title: Prevalence and Associated Risk Factors for Compassion Fatigue Among Family Caregivers of People Living with Cancer in Kitui, Kenya
content: With more than 20 million new cases and 9.8 million deaths in 2024, cancer remains among the leading causes of morbidity and mortality, globally. The increasing burden has increased patients’ reliance on family caregivers who often provide long physical and emotional support, thereby rendering them vulnerable to compassion fatigue (CF). However, prevalence of CF and associated factors remain limited, especially in Kenya. Therefore, this study determined the prevalence of CF and associated risk factors among family caregivers of patients living with cancer attending the Phangisile Mtshali Cancer Centre in Kitui, Kenya. An analytic cross‐sectional study was conducted among 462 family caregivers. Data was collected from April to July using a digitized modified Zarit Burden Interview Tool and analyzed in R Version 4.4.1. Most participants (57.4%) were females, and CF prevalence was 85.0%. Age 30-39 years (OR=0.19, 95%CI: 0.05–0.77, p =0.02) and being a parent caring for a child (OR=4.49, 95%CI: 1.05-19.17, p=0.043) were significantly associated with mild-moderate compassion fatigue. Being female, caregiving duration (13-24 months), and patient functional level (required assistance, completely dependent) were associated with high compassion fatigue (OR=2.44, 95% CI: 1.16-5.12, p=0.019; (OR= 0.24, 95% CI: 0.08-0.72, p=0.01; OR=8.17, 95% CI: 3.70-18.05, p =<0.001; OR=3.67, 95%CI: 1.14-11.80, p=0.029) respectively.  This study revealed a high prevalence of compassion fatigue in this population. Furthermore, the study has provided key strategic information to guide the development of targeted interventions.
